import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 46

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/46](https://www.erdosproblems.com/46)
- [Cr03] Croot, III, Ernest S., *On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions*. Ann. of Math. (2)
  (2003), 545-556.
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
-/

namespace Erdos46

/--
Does every finite colouring of the integers have a monochromatic solution to
$1=\sum \frac{1}{n_i}$ with $2\leq n_1<\cdots <n_k$?

The answer is yes, as proved by Croot [Cr03] - indeed, there are infinitely many disjoint such
monochromatic solutions.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos46.lean"]
theorem erdos_46 :
    answer(True) ↔
    -- For any finite colouring of the integers
    ∀ (𝓒 : ℕ → ℕ), (Set.range 𝓒).Finite →
      -- there are integers `2 ≤ n₁ < ⋯ < n_k`
      ∃ S : Finset ℕ, (∀ n ∈ S, 2 ≤ n) ∧
        -- whose reciprocals sum to `1`
        ∑ n ∈ S, (1 / n : ℚ) = 1 ∧
        -- and which all have the same colour
        (𝓒 '' (S : Set ℕ)).Subsingleton := by
  sorry

/--
Croot [Cr03] proved more: there are infinitely many disjoint such monochromatic solutions.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_46.variants.infinitely_many_disjoint :
    answer(True) ↔
    ∀ (𝓒 : ℕ → ℕ), (Set.range 𝓒).Finite →
      ∃ S : ℕ → Finset ℕ, (∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (S i) (S j)) ∧
        ∀ i, (∀ n ∈ S i, 2 ≤ n) ∧ ∑ n ∈ S i, (1 / n : ℚ) = 1 ∧
          (𝓒 '' (S i : Set ℕ)).Subsingleton := by
  sorry

/--
In [ErGr80] they also ask for a monochromatic representation of any $\frac{a}{b}>0$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_46.variants.positive_rat :
    answer(True) ↔
    ∀ (𝓒 : ℕ → ℕ), (Set.range 𝓒).Finite → ∀ q : ℚ, 0 < q →
      ∃ S : Finset ℕ, (∀ n ∈ S, 2 ≤ n) ∧ ∑ n ∈ S, (1 / n : ℚ) = q ∧
        (𝓒 '' (S : Set ℕ)).Subsingleton := by
  sorry

end Erdos46

reformulations.difference: Uses finite-range colourings ℕ → ℕ and an unordered Finset ℕ instead of a finite colouring of the integers and strictly increasing denominators.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Finite colour palettes can be relabelled by natural numbers, and a finite-range colouring can be relabelled by Fin r. Restricting a colouring of ℤ to ℕ, or extending a colouring of ℕ using Int.toNat, preserves all relevant denominators because they are at least 2. Sorting the finset gives the source's strictly increasing sequence; conversely, strict monotonicity makes the sequence's image a finset with the same sum. These equivalences were proved in scratch.lean.

reformulations.difference: Encodes infinitely many disjoint solutions as an ℕ-indexed pairwise-disjoint sequence, without separately asserting injectivity or one common colour for the entire family.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every solution is nonempty because its reciprocal sum is 1. Pairwise disjointness therefore forces the sequence to be injective, yielding an infinite family. Conversely, an infinite family has a countably infinite subfamily. If the source is read as requiring all solutions to share one colour, finite-range colouring and infinite pigeonhole give such a subsequence. Both the infinite-family equivalence and the common-colour equivalence were proved in Lean.

reformulations.difference: The colour may depend on q in Lean. Erdős–Graham, p. 37, asks whether “one class” contains integers whose reciprocals sum to “each rational” a/b, suggesting a single colour working for all positive rationals.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The universally quantified statements are equivalent, although the quantifiers cannot simply be interchanged for an arbitrary relation. The Lean statement's q = 1 case gives the universal colouring theorem. Recolouring any finite forbidden set with private colours forces a unit-sum solution to avoid it, yielding infinitely many disjoint solutions. Apply this to n ↦ c(k!·n). For each k, infinite pigeonhole supplies one colour with infinitely many disjoint sums equal to 1/k!. Some colour recurs for infinitely many k. Given q = m/d > 0, choose such a k ≥ d and unite m·k!/d disjoint solutions; their sum is q in that same colour. The converse forgets the uniform colour. The full equivalence is proved as ReviewErdos46.rational_uniform_equiv, with no sorryAx dependency.
